reads: the first is Dr. Roylott’s, the second my sister’s, and the third my own
text: Three ground-floor bedrooms in a row: Roylott's, Julia's, Helen's. If they lie in that order, Julia's room is in the middle, with Roylott's on one side and Helen's on the other.

reads: There is no communication between them, but they all open out into the same corridor
text: No connecting doors between the bedrooms. The shared corridor is the only link.

reads: Do I make myself plain?
text: A floor plan given with 'Do I make myself plain?' is meant to be used later. I will keep the room order and the single corridor in mind.

reads: The windows of the three rooms open out upon the lawn.
text: All three windows face the lawn, so anyone on the lawn is outside every bedroom at once.
Smoke and smell travel only where air can pass: an open window, a gap under a door, some opening. A truly sealed wall will not carry them.
exceptions: A smell can come round by the corridor or under a door without any hidden opening.

reads: my sister was troubled by the smell of the strong Indian cigars which it was his custom to smoke
text: Roylott was awake in his room that night, smoking. The smell reached Julia's room and drove her to Helen's.

Cigar smoke got from Roylott's room into Julia's, though the rooms 'have no communication'. It may only have come round by the corridor, but it is a small sign that air passes between the rooms somehow.

reads: she sat for some time, chatting about her approaching wedding
text: Until eleven Julia was well and talking happily about her wedding.

reads: during the last few nights I have always, about three in the morning, heard a low, clear whistle
text: For the last few nights Julia has been woken around 3 a.m. by a low, clear whistle.

reads: I cannot tell where it came from—perhaps from the next room, perhaps from the lawn
text: Julia cannot say whether the whistle came from the next room or from the lawn.
Where does the whistle come from? Julia's 'next room' would be Roylott's or Helen's, and the lawn lies under all three windows.
options: Helen's room (she denies whistling in her sleep)
The lawn or plantation, i.e. the gipsies

text: The whistle began only 'the last few nights', as the wedding drew near, though she had been engaged for months. Something may have started just before the wedding.

reads: It must be those wretched gipsies in the plantation.
text: Helen reaches for the gipsies at once, as the neighbourhood would. It is a ready explanation, not evidence, and why gipsies would whistle at 3 a.m. under the windows is not clear.
A light sleeper wakes at sounds a heavy sleeper sleeps through, so one person's not hearing a noise is weak evidence that it did not occur.

reads: I sleep more heavily than you
text: Helen's not hearing the whistle proves little, since Julia is the light sleeper. Julia's own doubt, that a whistle on the lawn would have woken Helen too, pushes slightly towards a source nearer Julia.
The 'next room' next to Julia is Roylott's or Helen's, and Helen denies whistling in her sleep. If Julia's guess is right, the whistle came from Roylott's room, which is weak but worth holding.

reads: a few moments later I heard her key turn in the lock
text: Helen heard Julia lock her own door from inside at about eleven.

reads: We had no feeling of security unless our doors were locked
text: The sisters always locked themselves in, and the reason Helen gives is the cheetah and baboon.
Two girls living with a violent man lock their doors, and only the animals are named as the reason. The animals are the polite reason, and the locks would also keep out the man.

reads: The wind was howling outside, and the rain was beating and splashing against the windows
text: A gale and heavy rain that night. Small noises would be hard to judge.

reads: A vague feeling of impending misfortune impressed me
text: Helen's premonition, and her talk of twins' 'subtle links', are feelings told afterwards. They carry no evidence about what happened.

reads: there burst forth the wild scream of a terrified woman
text: A scream in the night that Helen knew at once for Julia's, and she ran into the corridor.

reads: As I opened my door I seemed to hear a low whistle, such as my sister described, and a few moments later a clanging sound, as if a mass of metal had fallen
text: After the scream, as Helen opened her door, she seemed to hear the whistle and then a metallic clang. 'Seemed' marks her own doubt.
The whistle came after Julia's scream, not before it. So the whistle did not wake or startle her this time. It may be a signal given once the harm was done, or a coincidence.
options: A signal made after the thing was done
An unrelated noise of the night

reads: my sister’s door was unlocked, and revolved slowly upon its hinges
text: Julia's door, locked from inside at eleven, came open slowly and Julia stumbled out. She must have unlocked it herself, and Helen saw no one else.

reads: She writhed as one who is in terrible pain, and her limbs were dreadfully convulsed
text: Julia was convulsed and in pain, then lost consciousness, and she died without recovering it.

reads: It was the band! The speckled band!
text: Julia's last words: 'It was the band! The speckled band!' The past tense says she saw or met something definite.
A dying person's last words often name what they last saw or whom they fear, but pain and delirium can scramble them.
exceptions: Words in convulsion may mean little.

text: What is a 'speckled band'?
options: A band of people, e.g. the gipsies
A band of cloth: a ribbon, headcloth or strap
Something marked or banded, perhaps a creature
hindsight: The third option needs a first-time reader to take 'band' as a stripe or coil on something living; knowing the ending makes it look obvious.

reads: she stabbed with her finger into the air in the direction of the Doctor’s room
text: Her words may say what she met and her pointing where it came from, or point at the man. Either way her last act was to point at Roylott's room, not at the window or lawn.

reads: I met him hastening from his room in his dressing-gown
text: Roylott came out of his room in a dressing-gown, poured brandy down her throat, and sent for medical help. Julia died without recovering consciousness.

reads: I rushed out, calling loudly for my stepfather
text: Julia's scream was heard by Helen amid the gale, yet Roylott, in the next room, comes only when Helen calls. It may only mean he was in bed or smoking, and I would not rest anything on it.

At eleven she was well and cheerful, and within hours she was dead after a sudden seizure with pain. That strains the idea of simple illness and leaves poison, violence, or some other cause to examine.

reads: are you sure about this whistle and metallic sound?
text: Holmes questions the whistle and the clang before the band. He treats those two sounds as the facts most worth testing.

reads: among the crash of the gale and the creaking of an old house, I may possibly have been deceived
text: Helen hedges. She had been told of the whistle only hours earlier, so she may have heard what she expected, and the gale makes it worse. The clang is the sound no one had primed her for, so it is the better of the two.
A match burns out in seconds, so a person still holding the charred stump struck it moments before.
exceptions: A stump can be kept and carried for longer.

reads: In her right hand was found the charred stump of a match, and in her left a match-box
text: Julia was in her night-dress, holding a burnt-out match in one hand and the box in the other.
She struck a light in her room moments before she came out, so she was awake in the dark and wanted to see something. Whatever she saw or met was in the room, within seconds of her flight.
Why did she strike a light?
options: The whistle woke her and she went to look
Something touched or moved in the dark
A noise in the room alarmed her

reads: That is important
text: Holmes agrees she struck a light and looked about, and flags it. The match is a clue to read: she looked, and she saw something.
A door found fastened on the inside generally means nobody entered or left by it after it was fastened.
exceptions: A trick, a second key, or someone locking it from inside and leaving by another way.

reads: he was unable to find any satisfactory cause of death
text: A careful coroner found no cause of death, and he was not friendly to Roylott.

reads: The chimney is wide, but is barred up by four large staples
text: Julia's room was sealed in every way the coroner checked: door fastened inside, barred shutters secured nightly, walls sounded solid, floor examined, chimney barred. There were no marks of violence on her.

reads: It is certain, therefore, that my sister was quite alone when she met her end
text: No person came in by any way the inquiry knows. That means Roylott, the gipsies and any stranger were not in the room as ordinary intruders, and he cannot have struck her.
The door being fastened comes from Helen's own hearing. The state of walls, floor and shutters comes from an inspection afterwards, and Roylott's household had the room first.
The list never mentions the ceiling or any ventilation, nor what lay in the room. Nothing is said of anything fallen that would explain the 'mass of metal'.
The walls are 'quite solid all round', yet cigar smoke from Roylott's room reached Julia's. If both are true, something carried air between the rooms and the inspection missed it.
hindsight: The text gives no prompt linking the cigar smell to the sealed-room puzzle; a first-time reader needs the habit of asking how smoke crossed a solid wall.

text: The cheetah and baboon did not kill her. A sealed room and no marks on the body exclude a mauling. Some smaller or subtler creature is not excluded.
The gipsies and any stranger could not have got into a sealed room. If they are involved, it is only at a distance, such as a signal outside.
Not 'who got into the room' but 'what was already inside it, or what could pass through the barred window, the chimney or some gap that nobody listed'?
options: Something that passed a small opening

text: Roylott still has the motive, and Julia pointed at his room. But he did not strike her, so if he was the cause the means was indirect or hidden. Motive alone no longer carries it.

reads: How about poison?
text: Holmes goes straight to poison, which my own hypothesis about Roylott the doctor also raised.
In the 1880s chemical tests could find the common mineral and plant poisons but not every unusual one, so a negative result is weaker evidence than it sounds.
exceptions: Poisons used in real cases were usually of the common sorts, and findings were often clear.

reads: The doctors examined her for it, but without success.
text: Poison was looked for and not found. That weakens it, but does not kill it: convulsions with pain fit a poison, the tests have limits, and 'without success' says only that they found nothing.
Victorians accepted that a violent shock or fright could kill a person outright, and doctors and coroners said so.
exceptions: Later medicine held it rare in the young and healthy.

reads: It is my belief that she died of pure fear and nervous shock
text: Helen's belief fits the period's idea of death from fright. It is her theory, not a finding: the coroner found no cause.

reads: though what it was that frightened her I cannot imagine
text: Fright needs a thing that frightens. A sealed room with a match struck and a named 'band' means something frightened her inside it, which Helen cannot name. Her theory moves the puzzle but does not solve it.

reads: Were there gipsies in the plantation at the time?
text: Holmes tests the gipsy reading of 'band' and of the whistle, rather than assuming it.

reads: Yes, there are nearly always some there.
text: The gipsies are always there, so their presence that night proves nothing in particular. No one on the lawn was singled out.

reads: Sometimes I have thought that it was merely the wild talk of delirium
text: Helen offers two readings of 'band': delirium, or a band of people such as the gipsies in their spotted headcloths.

reads: the spotted handkerchiefs which so many of them wear over their heads
text: A headcloth would make a spotted 'band'. But no one could get into the locked room, and Julia pointed at the Doctor's room, not at the plantation. The gipsy reading fits the word and not the scene.
Delirium is the easy way out. Julia named a definite thing, had lit a match, and pointed. She spoke like someone who had just seen something.

Helen has steered to the gipsies twice (¶41, ¶64) and never says the plain thing, that Julia pointed at her stepfather. She lives under his roof and fears him, which may make her reluctant to accuse him aloud.

reads: These are very deep waters
text: Holmes shakes his head at both of Helen's readings and finds the case deep. I should not expect an easy solution.

Open: how Julia died in a sealed room; what the 'speckled band' is; where the whistle comes from and why it followed the scream; what clanged; what she saw by match light; how smoke crossed the wall; whether any unusual poison was missed; and what has newly frightened Helen.

Revised picture: Roylott still has the motive and the proximity (his room is next to Julia's), and Julia pointed at it. But nothing human entered, and the gipsies and big animals fall away. The likeliest line is some means from outside the room or already within it, with the whistle as a signal. The method is unknown.
options: Roylott used a hidden means: something sent or placed, with the whistle as a signal
A poison missed by the tests
Julia died of fright from something unconnected to Roylott

text: If Helen's danger repeats Julia's, her story should now bring in something new in her own recent nights, such as the whistle, the smoke or a change in the rooms, and that is what made her come this morning.
